1.pericope_label: Another angel lightens the earth; fallen, fallen is Babylon the great
debates: Who the descending angel is: Bede takes him for the Lord himself incarnate or else for the doctors of the Church; Clarke reads him as a human messenger of the everlasting gospel who by preaching and writings diffuses the light of truth; Robertson settles only that he is not the angel of the previous chapter who guided John; Ellicott declines the identification altogether and asks instead what the light does

Whether the doubled cry marks two falls: Henry reports the opinion that the repetition means first her apostasy and then her ruin, and rejects it on the ground that what follows describes her punishment rather than her sin, since unclean spirits and ominous birds were commonly supposed to haunt a city lying in ruins; Robertson takes the repeated aorists simply as a solemn dirge

What Babylon stands for: Clarke lists Rome pagan, Rome papal and Jerusalem without choosing; Barnes chooses the Papacy and guards the choice, that not the city but the power seated there is meant, so nothing need be looked for literally; Wesley argues from the Romanist premise against it; Gill restricts the drinking nations to the Roman empire and Europe, since the pagan and Mahometan nations have not drunk; Bede looks for no city at all, only the city of the devil
outliers: Robertson's borrowing of Swete, that so recently has the angel come from the Presence that in passing he flings a broad belt of light across the dark earth
Wesley's inference from the brightness of the messenger, that if such is the lustre of the servant no image could display the majesty of the Lord

The division over the word rendered hold, which Barnes and Robertson take as watch-post or garrison and Ellicott renders prison, with Robertson adding Swete's image of evil spirits building their eyries in the broken towers
Gill's question why the voice must be loud, answered from the deep sleep and spirit of slumber in which Babylon will be insensible of her ruin until it comes
Bede's gloss on the merchants, that he calls those rich in sins who by an infelicitous traffic exchange their souls for temporal abundance, excess of luxuries making poor instead of rich
Robertson's observation that here alone in the New Testament do we catch a glimpse of the vast traffic between east and west that made Rome rich

4.pericope_label: Come out of her, my people; her plagues come in one day
debates: Whether the sins reaching heaven are a heap or a cry: Ellicott takes the image literally as a heap firmly fastened and towering like another Babel, and says expressly that this is more than the cry of sin reaching heaven as at Sodom, since the sins themselves have touched the face of heaven; Barnes denies exactly that, holding the meaning is not a pile but that the guilt had become prominent enough to attract God’s attention, and compares the blood of Abel crying from the ground; Robertson and Gill settle the philology in Ellicott’s favour without arguing it, the verb deriving from the word for glue

What coming out of her requires: Ellicott insists it is not a bodily exodus from Rome but separation from the spirit of the world, though it may sometimes lead to a literal exodus and even to secession from a world-corrupted church; Barnes presses the practical edge harder, that the command not only justifies the Reformation but would have made a longer continuance in that communion an act of guilt once its wickedness was seen

Of what city the burning is spoken: Barnes argues at length that it may be more than figure and that Rome itself will literally be destroyed by fire, canvassing Jewish and early Christian expectation to that effect; Clarke refuses the whole application, observing that Rome pagan was never so treated since Alaric and Totilas burnt only parts of it, that Rome papal has not been so treated either, and that the description is true of Jerusalem, which is not generally thought to be intended
outliers: The spread of opinion on whose voice it is, from Wesley’s flat identification with Christ through Barnes's and Gill's leaning toward God to Ellicott's refusal of the question as unnecessary
Clarke's substitution of a couplet from Mantuanus for an argument, that those who desire to live a godly life should depart, since at Rome all things are lawful except to be good

Ellicott's double correction of the received text at the call for recompense, that the word rendered you should be omitted since it is not the saints who repay her, and that the double does not mean double her sins
Robertson's note that the double recompense was according to the Levitical law, against Wesley's reduction of it to a full retaliation by Hebrew idiom

Gill's naming of the executioners as the seven angels and the ten kings, and his particular that as she burnt many of the precious saints in the flames, as here in England, so shall she be utterly burnt
Ellicott's arrangement of the plagues as a fourfold answer, death for her scorn of widowhood, mourning for her revelling, famine for her abundance, and fire for her fornication
themes: come out of her, my people

9.pericope_label: The kings bewail her afar off; the merchants weep, for no man buyeth
debates: Whether the catalogue of merchandise is to be read literally: Gill argues sharply that it cannot be, since such commodities if they do not sell at one place will sell at another, the decline of trade in one city does not stop business the world over, and the ruin of commerce in one place is often the rise of it in another, so that these things will be merchandised somewhere to the end of the world; Barnes treats the enumeration far more lightly, as filling out the representation of what is found in such a city; Robertson takes it as documentary, counting twenty-nine items of import into the port of Rome and citing Galen, Pliny and Aristides on the commerce that made Rome the world’s chief market

Why the mourners stand afar off: Henry makes it a moral, that Babylon’s friends were willing to share her pleasures but not her plagues; Barnes reads it as impotence, that those who sustained the power will not even attempt to rescue it; Gill offers incapacity and dread together without choosing; Robertson alone describes fascination rather than fear, that there is a weird charm in a burning city, and compares Nero’s delight in the burning of Rome

What the lament is really about: Henry and Ellicott agree that the sorrow is worldly, but reach it differently, Henry by observing that they lament their ruin and not their idolatry, luxury or persecution, and Ellicott by analysing the grief as fear mingled with selfishness; Barnes turns the same verse political, that the kings of Europe owed their influence to this power and that its fall will be the signal for a general overturning of the thrones of Europe
outliers: Henry's identification of what the two classes of mourners had gained, the kings being suffered to be arbitrary and tyrannical over their subjects so long as they were obsequious, the merchants trafficking for indulgences, pardons, dispensations and preferments

Ellicott's description of the architecture of the three laments, each mourner standing afar off, each beginning with an Alas, and the words in one hour recurring with the monotony of a passing bell heard at intervals amid the strains of sad music
Wesley's philological aside that Rome was anciently termed by its inhabitants Valentia, that is strong, and that the name Rome itself signifies strength in Greek
Gill's second argument, that restricting the loss to Rome and its neighbourhood will not help either, since goods unsold there could be sold elsewhere and would not warrant so great a lamentation
Robertson's observation of how closely the list of items follows the destruction of Tyre in Ezekiel

Clarke's abandonment of comment in favour of a long paraphrase of Bishop Bale, in which her mitred merchants and soul-sellers wax rich by the sale of oils, cream, ashes, palm, wax, beads, crosses, bells, organs, images, relics and other pedlary wares
themes: in one hour is thy judgment come

12.pericope_label: The merchandise of Babylon; slaves and souls of men; the fruits departed
debates: Whether the cargo is Roman trade or an allegory of church wares: Robertson treats it as documentary and glosses the items from ancient sources, and Barnes runs the same course with Gibbon at his elbow; Gill runs a literal and a mystical reading together, taking the merchandise both for the riches which the Roman clergy bring into their coffers and for the doctrines of the gospel which they pretended to deliver while putting off wood and hay and stubble; Clarke abandons his own comment and prints a long stretch of Bishop Bale itemising the pontifical rings, censers and mitres

Whether bodies and souls of men are one article or two: Robertson insists the first word means simply bodies, treated as animals or implements alongside the horses and chariots, cites the usage from Genesis, Tobit and Maccabees, and suggests the following conjunction should be rendered even rather than and, making the two phrases one; Barnes reports the narrower construction of Stuart, that the word means grooms, a class of slaves employed about horses and carriages; Wesley keeps the phrases apart and makes the second the worse, that souls of men are continually bought and sold at Rome

What the fruits are: Barnes and Clarke take the noun from the season, the late summer or dog-days when the fruits ripen, and refer it to any fruit brought as a luxury into a great city; Wesley insists the turn is domestic, that the vision passes from imports to the home delicacies of Rome, and that the word covers pears, peaches, nectarines and all of the apple and plum kinds; Gill takes it mystically, of the universal dominion and the obedience of kings of which a large harvest was expected
outliers: Robertson's derivation of the silk from the people from whom the fabric came after Alexander invaded India, and his description of thyine as an odoriferous North African citrus prized for a grain like a peacock's tail or the stripes of a tiger

Barnes's repeated appeal to Gibbon, that pearls claimed the first rank after the diamond among the luxuries of Rome and that a variety of aromatics was consumed in religious worship and the pomp of funerals
Gill's citation of Brightman that Spain fetches these wares from the Indies for Rome as Italy fetches the spices from Greece, Arabia and Egypt

Gill's mystical turn on the cinnamon, that being used by harlots to perfume their bed it refers to the licensed brothels of Rome, each woman paying so much a week, the revenues sometimes reaching twenty thousand ducats a year
Robertson's note that the slave merchant was named a body-merchant, and his borrowing of Swete's phrase human live stock
Wesley's observation that the word for chariots is purely Latin inserted into the Greek, which he thinks John used on purpose in describing the luxury of Rome

15.pericope_label: The merchants and mariners stand afar off; rejoice over her, thou heaven
debates: Whether the finery of verse sixteen is worn or sold: Barnes takes the city as personified, so that what were articles of traffic now clothe her as a woman dressed in the richest of them; Clarke denies it on lexical grounds, that the verb rendered clothed often signifies to abound or be laden with, as the best Greek writers use it and as Kypke shows, and that these are therefore not personal ornaments but the articles of trade in which the city trafficked

What the text of verse seventeen reads: Barnes finds the received reading giving the whole company in ships while the editors he follows give one who sails to a place, that is a coaster who does not venture far out to sea and so a lesser class of seafarer; Clarke prefers the same reading and explains the practice behind it, that in those times the compass being unknown every voyage was performed coastwise within sight of land; Robertson notes Nestle’s further conjecture of sea for place and declines it as unnecessary

Whether the naming of apostles in heaven bears on the date and authorship of the book: Ellicott alone raises the argument, that because the verse names apostles in heaven some have inferred the twelve were all dead before the Apocalypse was written and therefore John did not write it, and answers that the verse states nothing about who has passed into heaven but is simply a summons to all who fought on their Lord’s side
outliers: Barnes's reconciliation of the one day of the earlier verse with the one hour here, that the shorter term is what the ruin seemed to the lookers-on
Gill's proverb that the Jews said if ten measures of riches descended into the world the ancient Romans took nine and the whole world the tenth
Robertson's single sentence on the smoke, that the eternal city is eternal no longer
Wesley's principle that most of the expressions describing this downfall are taken from Ezekiel's description of the downfall of Tyre
Barnes's insistence that the summons to rejoice is not the language of vengeance but of exultation that the cause of truth may now spread without hindrance

Robertson's observation that the verb for rejoicing here is the same used earlier of the joy of the wicked over the death of the two witnesses, and that the word for judgment means a case brought to trial rather than a sentence
themes: in one hour so great riches

21.pericope_label: The millstone cast into the sea; found no more at all; the blood of prophets
debates: Whether the prophecy has been fulfilled: Clarke twice denies it, holding that the words are true of ancient Babylon, whose very site is uncertain, and true of Jerusalem, but not true of Rome pagan nor as yet of Rome papal, which still exists, so that there is no city to which all these things are yet applicable and the prophecy must remain to be fulfilled; Barnes applies the whole chapter firmly to Papal Rome as the course of the preceding interpretation demands, and Gill and Wesley assume that application throughout

How far the blood-guilt reaches: Barnes takes the charge nearly at face value, that persecution there was so constant that all the blood ever shed may be said to have been poured out there; Ellicott denies the literal sense expressly, holding that the world city is founded on principles whose logical outcome is violence and that those who die by her hands, few or many, are evidence of the tendency of her power, and draws the rule that in the heavenly view we are guilty of all that the spirit of our conduct tends to do; Wesley piles up numbers instead and then concedes the figure may be overcharged

Who the mighty angel is: Gill will have him neither Christ nor a ministering spirit but some man or set of men; Barnes takes him for an angel distinct from the one at the head of the chapter; Ellicott is concerned only that he is strong enough to lift the ponderous stone
outliers: Ellicott's reading of the great dead mass sinking helplessly by the law of its own weight as a fall past recovery, and his antithesis that she who sat as a queen upon many waters sinks as a stone in the mighty waters

Clarke's attention to the mechanics, that the stone falls with the accelerated force of gravitation and with that force greatly increased by the projectile force impressed upon it by the destroying angel

The independent counting of the refrain, Ellicott finding the words no more repeated six times like a funeral knell and Robertson counting the same negatives grammatically as a fourfold sonorous repetition with two more following

Wesley's reading of the silences as a social ladder, music being the entertainment of the rich, trade the business of the middle rank, the preparing of bread the employment of the lowest, and marriage the means by which cities are peopled, so that no rank could live there any more

Robertson's excursus from the Greek word for sorcery to its English descendant, and his examples of quackery in patent medicines, witch-doctors and professional faith-healers, true medical science having had a hard fight to shake off charlatanry

Gill's retribution on the candle, that where wax candles burned in daylight there will not be one to give light at night, and where candles were lighted for the dead there will not be one for the living
themes: the millstone cast into the sea
the blood of prophets and saints
